title: Woman who was beaten by her ex-husband says 'life could've been in jeopardy' after N.L. justice department didn't tell her about his release
summary: A survivor of intimate partner violence says no one told her in advance that her attacker was out of prison, even though she was registered with Victim Services. The Department of Justice and Public…

image.caption: The Danny Williams Building in Corner Brook, which opened in 2010, is home to Provincial and Supreme Courts. (Bernice Hillier/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador

A survivor of intimate partner violence says no one told her in advance that her attacker was out of prison, even though she was registered with Victim Services. The Department of Justice and Public Safety won't comment on the specific case but says, if a victim has asked for information about an inmate's release, "attempts will be made to inform the victim."
Women's advocate says missteps in Western Newfoundland case are concerning
A woman in western Newfoundland who endured assault, threats and harassment from her former husband says the justice system has let her down.
The survivor of intimate partner violence says she learned about her attacker's release from prison after he was already out.
The woman, referred to as PB in court documents, says she feels her safety was jeopardized by the lack of information.
"There were three full days there that my life could have been in jeopardy, and I didn't know," the woman told CBC.
"I would have been on high alert. I wouldn't have had my guard down. I wouldn't have walked my dog."
CBC is not identifying the woman, whose identity was protected by a publication ban during the legal proceedings.
Judge had 'grave concerns'
The case of intimate partner violence made headlines in June of this year when Judge Wayne Gorman included an order of banishment in his sentencing of the offender he identified as DM.
DM was sentenced to one year imprisonment, and an order to not be in Corner Brook nor Mount Moriah during his three years' probation.

In his written ruling, Gorman said he was imposing the little-used restriction of banishment because of his "grave concerns" about the safety of PB, based on the "extremely violent" assault in 2025 that left her seriously injured, as well as on DM's failure to abide by the conditions of his release after his time in prison for that crime.
In October 2025, DM had been convicted of assault and assault causing bodily harm as well as failure to comply with release orders and breaches of recognizances.

blocks.text: After being released and reoffending, DM was convicted in June 2026 on a charge of uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm, as well as a charge of criminal harassment and breaches of court and probation orders.
In his sentence in the most recent case, Judge Wayne Gorman said he was concerned that the man "will seriously harm PB."
Gorman imposed a higher sentence than what both the Crown and defence counsel had recommended, which was for 90 days of incarceration.

"DM's offences illustrate a concerning and extremely dangerous pattern: acts of violence and harassment against a former partner, combined with a refusal to comply with no-contact conditions in court orders," wrote Gorman.
"This persistence is frightening and we need not ignore what our experience tells us as to where this might lead," said Gorman in his ruling.
PB said it was a relief to know the judge took her situation so seriously, and she said it was a victory for all victims.
"Judge Gorman, in reading his sentencing, he really did take seriously the amount of danger that myself and my children are in from him, and how dangerous he actually is," said PB.
Victim wasn't told about release
However, PB's sense of safety was shattered again, earlier than she'd expected.
In August, after serving the minimum one-sixth of his sentence, DM applied for temporary absence, as he was entitled to do at that point in his sentence.

Victim Services called to tell PB about the application. But she was not informed when DM was approved for release, nor when he was released to a halfway house an hour's drive away from where PB lives. The woman only learned that information when she called back to inquire about the outcome of DM's application for temporary absence.
Paula Sheppard is the executive director of the Corner Brook Status of Women Council. (CBC)

Paula Sheppard, executive director of the Corner Brook Status of Women, said that's not adequate, and that PB deserved better. Sheppard made inquiries as soon as she found out about the inmate's release, and the man was subsequently transferred to a halfway house in St. John's.
"As someone who supports victims of violence, I think there have been so many missteps in this case that really contribute to ongoing safety concerns for the victim and their family," said Sheppard.

Sheppard said she believes PB should have been given ample notice to be able to reiterate her victim impact statement before the decision was made on a temporary release, and she should have been informed before the offender got out of prison.
Ruling should have made a difference: advocate
Sheppard also said she believes the stern warning in Gorman's sentencing ruling should have led justice officials to be more cautious about DM's case.

She said even after many years working in the field of women's advocacy, she's surprised that Gorman's ruling didn't have more of an influence on the decision about a temporary absence for the offender after serving the minimum required under the law.

"Given how public this case has been, how stern the warnings really were from the judge and the fact that he had publicly said that there were grave concerns,...to see that that wasn't considered is quite concerning," said Sheppard.
Attempts supposed to be made to inform victim
The Department of Justice and Public Safety said it can't comment on specific cases because of privacy concerns.
However, in a statement, the Department said: "In general, inmates are eligible to apply for a temporary absence after serving a portion of their sentence."

The department said that a classification officer investigates to determine if an inmate will be approved for a temporary absence and, if a victim has registered with Victim Services, that agency may be contacted to give input before an absence is granted.
The department said if a victim has requested information about an offender's release, "attempts will be made to inform the victim."

Sheppard recommends that there be mandatory reporting to victims of intimate partner violence with regard to applications, approvals and conditions for the release of offenders, and that victim safety be put at the forefront.
